title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet

epigraph.quote: Net profit is a story told by accrual accounting; cash flow from operations is the audit of whether customers actually paid for the story.
epigraph.author: Forensic Accounting Maxim

web_blocks.html: Across FY20 through FY26 (plus TTM to September 2026), Kross Limited's P&L shows strong sales growth and steady margin gains. Sales rose from ₹160 Cr in FY20 to ₹673 Cr in FY26 and ₹822 Cr TTM [1]. Operating margin climbed from 10% (FY20–FY22) to 12% (FY23) and held at 13% across FY24–TTM [1]. Lower post-IPO interest (down from ₹15 Cr in FY24 to ₹8 Cr in FY26) helped net profit grow from ₹2 Cr in FY20 to ₹55 Cr in FY26 and ₹69 Cr TTM [1]. Meanwhile, yearly depreciation rose from ₹4 Cr in FY23 to ₹9 Cr in FY26 and ₹11 Cr TTM [1].

web_blocks.title: Balance Sheet Leverage, CWIP & Equity Dilution

web_blocks.html: From March 2020 to September 2026, Kross's balance sheet went through a sharp leverage cycle. Reserves jumped from ₹120 Cr (Mar 2024) to ₹402 Cr (Mar 2025) after the ₹250 Cr IPO fresh issue, cutting debt from ₹118 Cr to ₹34 Cr [1][5]. Yet heavy plant additions lifted Fixed Assets plus CWIP from ₹111 Cr (Mar 2024) to ₹223 Cr (Mar 2026) and ₹277 Cr (Sep 2026) [1][3]. CWIP jumped from ₹16.0 Cr to ₹54.9 Cr, alongside ₹50.3 Cr in Other Non-Current Assets [3]. With Other Assets rising to ₹451 Cr, total borrowings climbed back to ₹119 Cr by September 2026 (₹77.9 Cr non-current, ₹39.2 Cr current, plus ₹1.6 Cr leases) [1][3]. On the Q2 FY27 call, management confirmed drawing the remaining ~₹50 Cr Mill 219 term loan will lift March 2027 gross debt to ~₹165–170 Cr [9]. India Ratings affirmed Kross at 'IND A' / Stable in June 2026 (0.72x FY26 net adjusted leverage), flagging working capital and net leverage above 2.0x [7]. On October 30, 2026, Kross allotted 15,00,000 shares at ₹212 (₹31.80 Cr) to non-promoters and 15,00,000 warrants at ₹212 (₹31.80 Cr) to promoters [12]. That brought ₹39.75 Cr upfront cash (₹23.85 Cr payable within 18 months), nudging promoter stake from 68.57% to 67.01% [1][12]. Kross paid zero dividends across FY20–FY26, keeping all earnings in the business [1].

web_blocks.title: Cash Conversion, Working Capital Stretch & ROCE Compression

web_blocks.html: The main red flag in Kross's accounts is the gap between Net Profit and Cash Flow from Operations (CFO). From FY24 through FY26, Kross posted ₹148 Cr of Net Profit (₹45 Cr + ₹48 Cr + ₹55 Cr) [1]. Yet cumulative CFO was only ₹45 Cr (₹8 Cr + ₹9 Cr + ₹28 Cr), a three-year CFO/PAT ratio of 30.4% [1]. CFO/EBITDA stood at just 23% in FY24, 22% in FY25, and 52% in FY26 [1]. After capex, Free Cash Flow was negative for three straight years: -₹19 Cr in FY24, -₹20 Cr in FY25, and -₹72 Cr in FY26 [1][11]. Crucially, the unaudited H1 FY27 cash flow statement (ended September 30, 2026) shows this gap widened further [3]. Against ₹33.16 Cr of H1 PAT (₹54.76 Cr pre-working-capital profit), H1 FY27 CFO fell to just ₹4.73 Cr (14.3% conversion, down from ₹5.09 Cr in H1 FY26) [3]. Other Current Assets jumped ₹23.89 Cr (to ₹54.32 Cr), Trade Receivables rose ₹9.12 Cr (to ₹206.29 Cr), and Other Current Financial Liabilities fell ₹5.24 Cr [3]. Subtracting ₹59.16 Cr of H1 PPE/CWIP capex yielded -₹54.43 Cr of H1 FY27 Free Cash Flow, funded by ₹64.77 Cr of net new borrowings [3].

The ratio ledger shows the cause. Working Capital Days rose from 19 days (FY23) and 30 days (FY24) to 106 days (FY25) and 124 days (FY26), matching Screener's alert on working capital jumping from 86.9 to 124 days [1]. Debtor Days jumped from 39 to 107, while Inventory Days rose from 78 to 105 [1]. Days Payable eased from 69 days in FY25 to 60 days in FY26, pushing the Cash Conversion Cycle to 153 days [1]. As receivables, inventory, and CWIP swelled capital employed, ROCE halved from 33% in FY24 to 22% in FY25 and 16% in FY26 (with ROE at 12.0%) [1]. That sits close to India's 12%–13% industrial cost of capital (WACC) until the seamless tube plant earns returns [1].

web_blocks.mechanism: North American commercial vehicle wheel-end, hub, and trailer parts supplier in a capital-heavy, OEM-led market. Heavy capex and debt service hit a freight downturn, cost inflation, and working-capital squeeze, draining cash to ~$6M.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: Filed Chapter 11 bankruptcy twice (Oct 2009 and Oct 9, 2024) with $500M–$1B in liabilities. Emerged in March 2025 after converting >$400M of debt to equity and wiping out prior shareholders.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: In truck and trailer parts, heavy capex, rising debt, and long working capital leave no buffer if a freight slump hits before new plants yield free cash flow.

web_blocks.title: Forensic Bottom Line: Earnings Quality vs. Capital Intensity
paragraphs: Kross's sales growth is real and backed by new plant lines, yet cash conversion remains weak: three-year FY24–FY26 CFO/PAT was 30.4% (-₹111 Cr cumulative FCF), and H1 FY27 CFO slipped further to ₹4.73 Cr (14.3% of ₹33.16 Cr PAT; -₹54.43 Cr H1 FCF).

Debtor Days must fall below 80 days, Other Current Assets (₹54.32 Cr) must unwind, and the ₹167–170 Cr Mill 219 seamless tube mill must turn CWIP into positive Free Cash Flow in FY28 as gross debt approaches ~₹165–170 Cr.

book_paragraphs: Now you and I do the part of fundamental analysis that separates real compounders from capital-hungry cyclicals: we follow the cash. On the surface, Kross Limited's seven-year income statement looks impressive. Sales climbed from ₹160 Cr in FY20 to ₹673 Cr in FY26 and ₹822 Cr on a trailing twelve-month basis, operating margins stepped up from 10% to 13%, and net profit compounded from ₹2 Cr to ₹55 Cr in FY26 with zero dividends paid out.

When you turn to the cash flow statement and ratio ledger, however, a completely different story emerges. Across FY24, FY25, and FY26 combined, Kross reported ₹148 Cr of net profit—yet generated only ₹45 Cr of cash flow from operations. That is a 30.4% cash-conversion ratio over three full years. Why did more than two-thirds of reported profit fail to reach the bank? Because Debtor Days jumped from 39 days in FY23 to 107 days in FY25 and FY26, Inventory Days rose from 78 to 105, and Days Payable slipped from 69 to 60 in FY26, pushing the Cash Conversion Cycle to 153 days and Working Capital Days from 30 days in FY24 to 124 days in FY26. Worse, the unaudited H1 FY27 cash flow statement confirms no relief yet: against ₹33.16 Cr of H1 net profit, operating cash flow fell to just ₹4.73 Cr—a 14.3% conversion rate—after Other Current Assets surged ₹23.89 Cr to ₹54.32 Cr and Trade Receivables reached ₹206.29 Cr.

Layer ₹100 Cr of FY26 capital expenditure on top of ₹28 Cr of operating cash flow, and you get -₹72 Cr of Free Cash Flow in FY26 alone—and -₹111 Cr of cumulative Free Cash Flow across FY24 to FY26, followed by another -₹54.43 Cr of Free Cash Flow in H1 FY27 (₹4.73 Cr CFO minus ₹59.16 Cr capex). Meanwhile, Fixed Assets plus CWIP jumped from ₹111 Cr in March 2024 to ₹277 Cr by September 2026, gross debt is guided to rise from ₹119 Cr toward ~₹165–170 Cr by March 2027, and Return on Capital Employed halved from 33% in FY24 to 16% in FY26, barely clearing a standard Indian industrial cost of capital.

That is why our FAILURE_BASE_RATE parallel—Accuride Corporation in the United States—matters so much here. Accuride made commercial vehicle wheels, hubs, and trailer wheel-end assemblies. It had real factories and real OEM customers, yet heavy debt, capex, and a freight downturn squeezed its liquidity down to $6 million and forced it into Chapter 11 bankruptcy in both 2009 and October 2024, wiping out equity holders in a March 2025 debt-for-equity swap. Kross is nowhere near distress—its 'IND A' rating and ₹119 Cr of September 2026 debt (rising toward ~₹165–170 Cr by March 2027) against ₹110 Cr of trailing EBITDA remain manageable—but the mechanism is the exact same warning: if an M&HCV downcycle arrives while working capital stays stretched and Mill 219 is still ramping, cash flow tightens fast.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Why Pass 1 Stops at Conditional
paragraphs: Putting Chapters 1 through 6 together gives us an unambiguous price-blind conclusion: Kross Limited is a real, growing Tier-1 manufacturer with genuine engineering capability in extruded trailer axles, but 30% three-year cash conversion, 124-day working capital, halving ROCE, and renewed debt-plus-equity funding make it a cyclical conditional business rather than a proven cash compounder.

book_subsections.title: Why Reported Earnings Outran Cash Generation
paragraphs: If you only glanced at Kross’s income statement, you would see a textbook growth story: sales compounding from ₹160 Cr in FY20 to ₹673 Cr in FY26 and ₹822 Cr on a trailing-twelve-month basis, with operating margins holding steady around 12%–13% and five-year profit compounding above 60%. Accrual accounting rewards a company that ships more axles and books higher revenue.

Turn one page to the cash flow statement, however, and the picture tightens sharply. Across FY24, FY25, and FY26 combined, Kross generated ₹144 Cr of net profit—yet cumulative operating cash flow was only ₹44 Cr, a 30.4% CFO-to-PAT conversion rate. Where did the missing ₹100 Cr go? It went straight into financing 107 days of customer receivables and 105 days of steel and work-in-progress inventory.

book_subsections.title: The Accuride Warning and the Conditional Verdict
paragraphs: When a manufacturing business converts only 30% of its accounting profit into operating cash while simultaneously committing ₹100 Cr a year to heavy machinery capex, the math forces external funding. Cumulative free cash flow from FY24 through FY26 was -₹111 Cr, which explains why debt returned to ₹119 Cr by September 2026 and equity was diluted again in October 2026.

That exact combination—heavy capex, stretched working capital, and commercial vehicle cyclicality—is why our FAILURE_BASE_RATE parallel, Accuride Corporation in North America, ended in Chapter 11 restructuring twice despite owning real wheel-end manufacturing assets. Kross is nowhere near Accuride’s leverage crisis thanks to its modest 0.23x–0.32x debt-to-equity ratio and IND A rating, which is why our price-blind verdict is CYCLICAL_CONDITIONAL rather than a fundamental fail. Now that the business reality is locked without price bias, we can finally capture the market price in Chapter 7.

Think of the balance sheet as a stress-test buffer rather than a trophy. Right now, Kross’s 0.23x–0.32x debt-to-equity ratio gives it breathing room while the seamless tube mill finishes construction, and its H1 FY27 revenue surge to ₹419.4 Cr shows strong top-line momentum. Still, until operating cash flow catches up with reported net profit and free cash flow turns sustainably positive, every rupee of earnings must be discounted for the capital required to produce it.

Forensic accounting is not about hunting for fraud; most of the time, it is simply about measuring how much capital a growing business consumes to stand still. Over FY24–FY26, Kross reported ₹144 Cr of cumulative net profit, yet generated only ₹44 Cr of operating cash flow and -₹111 Cr of free cash flow after ₹155 Cr of cumulative capital expenditure.

Compare that against our Accuride Corporation failure base rate. Accuride collapsed into Chapter 11 twice because cyclical freight downturns collided with heavy capex and high leverage. Kross’s modest 0.23x–0.32x debt-to-equity ratio and IND A credit rating keep it far from distress, yet the cash-flow gap is real enough that we refuse to classify Kross as a structural compounder until free cash flow turns sustainably positive.

If you remember only one number from Chapter 6, make it 30.4%—the share of cumulative net profit that Kross converted into operating cash flow across FY24–FY26. Accounting earnings can flatter a cyclical manufacturer during a capex cycle, but cash conversion never lies.
That single metric is why we insist on seeing positive free cash flow before ever promoting Kross from a cyclical watch to a long-term compounder.

Put simply, the income statement shows an accelerating manufacturer, while the cash flow statement shows a capital-hungry cyclical—and in institutional underwriting, the cash flow statement always casts the deciding vote.
